Aaron and his sons were to abstain from these expressions of sorrow, “lest they should die and wrath come upon all the people.” Accordingly, we are not to seek the reason for this prohibition merely in the fact, that they would defile themselves by contact with the corpses, a reason which afterwards led to this prohibition being raised into a general law for the high priest (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.10-Lev.21.11">Lev 21:10-11</reference>). The reason was simply this, that any manifestation of grief on account of the death that had occurred, would have indicated dissatisfaction with the judgment of God; and Aaron and his sons would thereby not only have fallen into mortal sin themselves, but have brought down upon the congregation the wrath of God, which fell upon it through every act of sin committed by the high priest in his official position (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.3">Lev 4:3</reference>). “<hi type="italic">Your brethren,</hi> (namely) <hi type="italic">the whole house of Israel, may bewail this burning</hi>” (the burning of the wrath of Jehovah). Mourning was permitted to the nation, as an expression of sorrow on account of the calamity which had befallen the whole nation in the consecrated priests. For the nation generally did not stand in such close fellowship with Jehovah as the priests, who had been consecrated by anointing.
entries.101ed6d4a79f37e4e67ccea536e564cc468b9555: <reference osisRef="Lev.10.7">Lev 10:7</reference> <div eID="gen1273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1274" type="x-p"/> The latter were not to go away from the door (the entrance or court of the tabernacle), sc., to take part in the burial of the dead, lest they should die, for the anointing oil of Jehovah was upon them. The anointing oil was the symbol of the Spirit of God, which is a Spirit of life, and therefore has nothing in common with death, but rather conquers death, and sin, which is the source of death (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.21.12">Lev 21:12</reference>).
entries.62fcbad6bc236512445df11683609eb04c5e114e: <reference osisRef="Lev.10.8-Lev.10.11">Lev 10:8-11</reference> <div eID="gen1274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1275" type="x-p"/> And the Lord spake unto Aaron, saying, Jehovah still further commanded Aaron and his sons not to drink wine and strong drink when they entered the tabernacle to perform service there, on pain of death, as a perpetual statute for their generations (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.17">Exo 12:17</reference>), that they might be able to distinguish between the holy and common, the clean and unclean, and also to instruct the children of Israel in all the laws which God had spoken to them through Moses (ו...ו, <reference osisRef="Lev.10.10">Lev 10:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.10.11">Lev 10:11</reference>, <hi type="italic">et</hi>...<hi type="italic">et</hi>, both...and also). <hi type="italic">Shecar</hi> was an intoxicating drink made of barley and dates or honey. הל, <hi type="italic">profanus</hi>, common, is a wider or more comprehensive notion than טמא, unclean. Everything was common (profane) which was not fitted for the sanctuary, even what was allowable for daily use and enjoyment, and therefore was to be regarded as clean. The motive for laying down on this particular occasion a prohibition which was to hold good for all time, seems to lie in the event recorded in <reference osisRef="Lev.10.1">Lev 10:1</reference>, although we can hardly infer from this, as some commentators have done, that Nadab and Abihu offered the unlawful incense-offering in a state of intoxication. The connection between their act and this prohibition consisted simply in the rashness, which had lost the clear and calm reflection that is indispensable to right action.
entries.7ab0371a0b771f7e14607aae08acec7ff4f760b3: <reference osisRef="Lev.10.12-Lev.10.18">Lev 10:12-18</reference> <div eID="gen1275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1276" type="x-p"/> After the directions occasioned by this judgment of God, Moses reminded Aaron and his sons of the general laws concerning the consumption of the priests’ portions of the sacrifices, and their relation to the existing circumstances: first of all (<reference osisRef="Lev.10.12">Lev 10:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.10.13">Lev 10:13</reference>), of the law relating to the eating of the meat-offering, which belonged to the priests after the <hi type="italic">azcarah</hi> had been lifted off (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.3">Lev 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.6.9-Lev.6.11">Lev 6:9-11</reference>), and then (<reference osisRef="Lev.10.14">Lev 10:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.10.15">Lev 10:15</reference>) of that relating to the wave-breast and heave-leg (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.32-Lev.7.34">Lev 7:32-34</reference>). By the <hi type="italic">minchah</hi> in <reference osisRef="Lev.10.12">Lev 10:12</reference> we are to understand the meal and oil, which were offered with the burnt-offering of the nation (<reference osisRef="Lev.9.4">Lev 9:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.9.7">Lev 9:7</reference>); and by the אשּׁים in <reference osisRef="Lev.10.12">Lev 10:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.10.15">Lev 10:15</reference>, those portions of the burnt-offering, meat-offering, and peace-offering of the nation which were burned upon the altar (<reference osisRef="Lev.9.13">Lev 9:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.9.17">Lev 9:17</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Lev.9.20">Lev 9:20</reference>). He then looked for “<hi type="italic">the he-goat of the sin-offering,</hi>” - i.e., the flesh of the goat which had been brought for a sin-offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.9.15">Lev 9:15</reference>), and which was to have been eaten by the priests in the holy place along with the sin-offerings, whose blood was not taken into the sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.19">Lev 6:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.22">Lev 6:22</reference>); - “<hi type="italic">and, behold, it was burned</hi>” (שׂרף,   3 <hi type="italic">perf</hi>. <hi type="italic">Pual</hi>). Moses was angry at this, and reproved Eleazar and Ithamar, who had attended to the burning: “<hi type="italic">Wherefore have ye not eaten the sin-offering in a holy place?</hi>” he said; “<hi type="italic">for it is most holy, and He </hi>(<hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>)<hi type="italic">hath given it you to bear the iniquity of the congregation, to make atonement for it before Jehovah,</hi>” as its blood had not been brought into the holy place (הוּבא construed as a passive with an accusative, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.4.18">Gen 4:18</reference>, etc.). “<hi type="italic">To bear the iniquity</hi>” does not signify here, as in <reference osisRef="Lev.5.1">Lev 5:1</reference>, to bear and atone for the sin in its consequences, but, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.28.38">Exo 28:38</reference>, to take the sin of another upon one’s self, for the purpose of cancelling it, to make expiation for it. As, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.28.38">Exo 28:38</reference>, the high priest was to appear before the Lord with the diadem upon his forehead, as the symbol of the holiness of his office, to cancel, as the mediator of the nation and by virtue of his official holiness, the sin which adhered to the holy gifts of the nation (see the note on this passage), so here it is stated with regard to the official eating of the most holy flesh of the sin-offering, which had been enjoined upon the priests, that they were thereby to bear the sin of the congregation, to make atonement for it. This effect or signification could only be ascribed to the eating, by its being regarded as an incorporation of the victim laden with sin, whereby the priests actually took away the sin by virtue of the holiness and sanctifying power belonging to their office, and not merely declared it removed, as <hi type="italic">Oehler</hi> explains the words (<hi type="italic">Herzog's</hi> Cycl. x. p. 649). <reference osisRef="Exod.28.38">Exo 28:38</reference> is decisive in opposition to the declaratory view, which does not embrace the meaning of the words, and is not applicable to the passage at all. “Incorporabant quasi peccatum populique reatum in se recipiebant” (<hi type="italic">Deyling observv. ss. </hi>i. 45, 2).<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">C. a Lapide</hi> has given this correct interpretation of the passage: “<hi type="italic">ut scilicet cum hostiis populi pro peccato simul etiam populi peccata in vos quasi recipiatis, ut illa expietis</hi>.” There is no foundation for the objection offered by <hi type="italic">Oehler</hi>, that the actual removal of guilt and the atonement itself were effected by the offering of the blood. For it by no means follows from <reference osisRef="Lev.17.11">Lev 17:11</reference>, that the blood, as the soul of the sacrificial animal, covered or expiated the soul of the sinner, and that the removal and extinction of the sin had already taken place with the covering of the soul before the holy God, which involved the forgiveness of the sin and the reception of the sinner to mercy.</note>
entries.50a7a52eebf3278eff705819f0f7ed2fbdf7753d: <reference osisRef="Lev.10.19-Lev.10.20">Lev 10:19-20</reference> <div eID="gen1276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1277" type="x-p"/> Aaron excused his sons, however, by saying, “<hi type="italic">Behold, this day have they offered their sin-offering and their burnt-offering, and this has happened to me,</hi>” i.e., the calamity recorded in Lev 10:1. has befallen me (קרא = קרה, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.42.4">Gen 42:4</reference>); “<hi type="italic">and if I had eaten the sin-offering to-day, would it have been well-pleasing to Jehovah?</hi>” וגו ואכלתּי is a conditional clause, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.33.13">Gen 33:13</reference>, cf. <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §357. Moses rested satisfied with this answer. Aaron acknowledged that the flesh of the sin-offering ought to have been eaten by the priest in this instance (according to <reference osisRef="Lev.6.19">Lev 6:19</reference>), and simply adduced, as the reason why this had not been done, the calamity which had befallen his two eldest sons. And this might really be a sufficient reason, as regarded both himself and his remaining sons, why the eating of the sin-offering should be omitted. For the judgment in question was so solemn a warning, as to the sin which still adhered to them even after the presentation of their sin-offering, that they might properly feel “that they had not so strong and overpowering a holiness as was required for eating the general sin-offering” (<hi type="italic">M. Baumgarten</hi>). This is the correct view, though others find the reason in their grief at the death of their sons or brethren, which rendered it impossible to observe a joyous sacrificial meal. But this is not for a moment to be thought of, simply because the eating of the flesh of the sin-offering was not a joyous meal at all (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.6.19">Lev 6:19</reference>).<note placement="foot">Upon this mistaken view of the excuse furnished by Aaron, <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> has founded his assertion, that “this section did not emanate from the Elohist, because he could not have written in this way,” an assertion which falls to the ground when the words are correctly explained.</note>  <chapter eID="Lev.10"/> <div eID="gen1277" type="x-p"/>

entries.a5cf27a83f5a3bd5384b5674501c12e97fe47d57: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.10.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.10.1" sID="gen18385" type="section"/><p/> <div sID="gen18386" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1. </hi><hi type="italic">And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron</hi> A memorable circumstance is here recorded, from whence it appears how greatly God abominates all the sins whereby the purity of religion is corrupted. Apparently it was a light transgression to use strange fire for burning incense; and again their thoughtlessness would seem excusable, for certainly Nadab and Abihu did not wantonly or intentionally desire to pollute the sacred things, but, as is often the case in matters of novelty, when they were setting about them too eagerly, their precipitancy led them into error. The severity of the punishment, therefore, would not please those arrogant people, who do not hesitate superciliously to criticise God’s judgments; but if we reflect how holy a thing God’s worship is, the enormity of the punishment will by no means offend us. Besides, it was necessary that their religion should be sanctioned at its very commencement; for if God had suffered the sons of Aaron to transgress with impunity, they would have afterwards carelessly neglected the whole Law. This, therefore, was the reason of such great severity, that the priests should anxiously watch against all profanation. Their crime is specified, viz., that they offered incense in a different way from that which God had prescribed, and consequently, although they may have erred from ignorance, still they were convicted by God’s commandment of having negligently set about what was worthy of greater attention. The “strange fire” is distinguished from the sacred fire which was always burning upon the altar: not miraculously, as some pretend, but by the constant watchfulness of the priests. Now, God had forbidden any other fire to be used in the ordinances, in order to exclude all extraneous rites, and to shew His detestation of whatever might be derived from elsewhere. Let us learn, therefore, so to attend to God’s command as not to corrupt His worship by any strange inventions. But if He so severely avenged this error, how horrible a punishment awaits the Papists, who are not ashamed obstinately to defend so many gross corruptions!<div eID="gen18386" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.10.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen18385" osisID="Lev.10.1" type="section"/>
entries.a181d525c9f29530667781781c3ffc4e0a3e311f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.10.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.10.3" sID="gen18387" type="section"/> <div sID="gen18388" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3. </hi><hi type="italic">Then Moses said unto Aaron, This is it that the Lord spake</hi> Moses restrains his brother from giving way to excessive grief; for this was a very bitter stroke after their recent joy to see himself at once deprived of two sons on the same day, and at the same moment, he might, too, have been disposed to murmur against God for the cause of their death. Lest, therefore, He should give way to such want of self-control, Moses reminds him that he must submit to the just judgment of God. We shall, however, seek in vain for what is here referred to, <note n="416"> <div sID="gen18389" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">A.</hi> <hi type="italic">V.,</hi> “I will be sanctified;” and so also <hi type="italic">C.’s</hi> own version; but he embodies the two clauses. Some, as De Lyra, refer this to <reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.19.22">Exodus 19:22</reference>; Others to <reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.43">Exodus 29:43</reference>. “Some think it was spoken, but not written, as many things beside. <hi type="italic">Oleaster,</hi> <hi type="italic">Lorinus,</hi> <hi type="italic">Caietan;</hi> but,” adds Willet, “they are of this mind, that they may have here some show for their unwritten traditions. Therefore,” he concludes, “without any more circumstance, we find this to have been spoken, <reference osisRef="Bible:Lev.8.35">Leviticus 8:35</reference>, ‘Keep ye the Lord’s charge, that ye die not;’ there they are commanded to observe the Lord’s ordinances, which he gave them, <hi type="italic">(Junius;)</hi> and because Nadab and Abihu did not so, they are punished with death.”<div eID="gen18389" type="x-p"/> </note> “I will be glorified in them that come nigh me.” He had often threatened the priests witlt death if they departed in the least degree from the prescribed rule: He had often set before them the sacredness of their office, lest they should defile themselves by any sacrilegious act; in a word, He had chosen them to be His ministers in holy things, on the condition that they should know themselves to be subject to greater guilt and punishment than the rest of the people. By this consolation, then, Aaron’s grief is quieted, that God had not dealt cruelly with his sons, but had shewn forth in them a just and profitable example, in order that their successors might be more attentive in their duties; for thus should the sentence be paraphrased: In order that I may be glorified before the whole people, I must be sanctified by those of the highest degree and consequence; or, When I shall have been sanctified by the priests themselves, whose dignity is the highest, my glory will shine forth before the whole people. And, in point of fact, although God may punish whole bodies of obscure persons, such lessons have but little effect; but the punishment of men of more noble and illustrious condition draws almost all eyes to the judgments of God. For God is said to be sanctified in us in many ways, whether He shews Himself to be a pitiful or a severe Judge. This declaration, then, is an exhortation to those whom he has dignified with peculiar honor, to walk in fear and trembling; for, since “judgment begins at the house of God,” the greater are the gifts and the higher the pre-eminence is with which any one is blessed, the greater is his obligation to God, and his ingratitude worthy of severer punishment.<div eID="gen18388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> <hi type="italic">And Aaron held his peace</hi> Much is this silence of Aaron to be applauded, whereby he confessed that his sons were slain by the just judgment of God; for Moses indicates that he yielded to his admonition, and was thus restrained from complaining against. God. Thus Paul teaches us that Scripture is given to teach us patience. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.15.4">Romans 15:4</reference>.) Wherefore, whenever our passions are too much excited, let us learn that this is the best remedy for quieting and repressing them, to <hi type="italic">submit</hi> <hi type="italic">ourselves</hi> <hi type="italic">to</hi> <hi type="italic">God,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">humble</hi> <hi type="italic">ourselves</hi> <hi type="italic">beneath</hi> <hi type="italic">his</hi> <hi type="italic">mighty</hi> <hi type="italic">hand.</hi> David invites us to this by his own example when he says,<div eID="gen18390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18391" type="x-p"/>“I was dumb, I opened not my mouth; because thou didst it.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.39.9">Psalm 39:9</reference>.)<div eID="gen18391" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.10.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen18387" osisID="Lev.10.3" type="section"/>
entries.a00dc3342c9bff06408c8a93622a1a1b1b0ae987: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.10.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.10.4" sID="gen18392" type="section"/> <div sID="gen18393" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4. </hi><hi type="italic">And Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan</hi> Lest Eleazar and Ithamar should carry <note n="417"> <div sID="gen18394" type="x-p"/> “Se polluassent en portant les corps morts de leurs freres;” should pollute themselves by carrying the dead bodies of their brothers. — <hi type="italic">Fr.</hi> Blunt has a very ingenious conjecture that Mishael and Elzaphan were the very persons “defiled by the dead body of a man,” mentioned in <reference osisRef="Bible:Num.9.6 Bible:Num.9.7">Numbers 9:6, 7</reference>, and who therefore could not keep the Passover. “The Veracity of the Five Books of Moses.” Art. 14. But surely, out of such a large body of persons, there must have been many deaths daily, and consequently others would have been defiled besides Mishael and Elzaphan.<div eID="gen18394" type="x-p"/> </note> forth the corpses, Moses commanded these others to anticipate them. It may also have been the case that all were stupified by terror. He forbids the father and brothers to mourn their death, not so much in accordance with the law, whereby all except the high priest were permitted to mourn for their own brother, as to prevent this memorable lesson from being obscured by their grief, since thus was the sanctity of their religion magnificently asserted. Nevertheless, God allowed the dead men to be bewailed by the people, lest the recollection of their punishment should too soon be lost.<div eID="gen18393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18395" type="x-p"/>When he forbids (Aaron <note n="418"> <div sID="gen18396" type="x-p"/> Added from <hi type="italic">Fr</hi>.<div eID="gen18396" type="x-p"/> </note> and his sons) to go out from the door of the tabernacle, he does not mean so to fix them to that place as to banish them from their own private tents, but he withholds them from all pollution which might have compelled them to desert or interrupt their duty.<div eID="gen18395" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.10.4" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen18392" osisID="Lev.10.4" type="section"/>

9. Do not drink wine, nor strong drink. The second cleanness required in the priests is that they should abstain from wine, and strong drink;
Lat., “sicera.” Fr, “ce qui est nomme en Hebrieu Sechar.” Blunt, “The veracity of the Books of Moses, etc.,” art. 13, argues on the probability of Nadab and Abihu’s sin in the offering of strange fire having been the effect of intoxication, from the fact of its relation being immediately followed by this prohibition. — Edit., 1835. Pp. 113, et seq.
Lorinus, however, in loco, refutes the notion from Tostatus, and so also Willet. It appears to have been of Jewish origin; and the principal arguments against it are, — 1. That it is not mentioned in the Scripture; and 2. That the offenders had been ministering from an early hour in the morning.
in which word Jerome says that everything intoxicating is included; and this I admit to be true; but the definition would be more correct, that all liquors espressed from fruits are denoted by it, in whose sweetness there is nearly as much to tempt men as in wine. Even in these days the Orientals compose of dates as well as of other fruits, liquors, which are exceedingly sweet and delicious. The same rule is, therefore, here prescribed for the priests, whilst in the performance of their duties, as for the Nazarites. Both were allowed freely to eat of all the richest foods; but God commanded them to be content with water, because abstinence in drinks very greatly conduces to frugality of living. For few are intemperate in eating, who do not also love wine; besides, an abundance of food generally satisfies the appetite, whilst there is no limit to drinking, where the love of wine prevails. Therefore, abstinence from wines was enjoined upon the priest, not only that they might beware of drunkenness, but that they might be temperate in eating, and not luxuriate in their abundance. But, inasmuch as sobriety is the main point in moderate living, God especially limited His priests in this respect, lest the rigor of their minds, and rectitude, and integrity of judgment, should be impaired by drinking. Hence it appears how great is man’s proneness to all defilements. Wine is very wholesome as one of our means of nutriment; but by the too free use of it many enervate their strength, becloud their understanding, and almost stupify all their senses so as to make themselves inactive. Some, too, degrade themselves into foul and brutish stupidity, or are driven by it to madness. Thus a pleasure, which ought to have incited them to give God thanks, is taken away from them on account of their vicious excess; and not without disgrace, because they know not how to enjoy God’s good gifts in moderation. He afterwards confirms the fact, that He interdicted wine to the priests when exercising their office, that they may distinguish “between clean and unclean,” and be sound and faithful interpreters of the Law. On this score it became them to be abstemious throughout their whole life, because they were always appointed to be masters to instruct the people; but lest immoderate strictness should tend to disgust them, so that they might be less disposed for the willing performance of the rest of their duty, God deemed it sufficient to admonish them by this temporary abstinence, that they should study to be sober at other times. Thus, then, it must be concluded that none are fit to teach who are given to gluttony, which corrupts the soundness of the mind, and destroys its rigor. The comment of Jerome is indeed a childish one, that “A fat belly does not engender a quick understanding:” for many corpulent men are of vigorous and active intellect, and indeed leanness is often the consequence of drinking too much. But those who stuff their bodies will never have sufficient activity of mind to execute the office of teaching. In conclusion, we gather from this passage, as Malachi says, (Malachi 2:7,) that the priests were interpreters of the Law, and messengers of the Lord of hosts, and not dumb masks For though the Law was written, yet God would ever have the living voice to resound in His Church, just as now-a-days preaching is inseparably united with Scripture.
Concerning the High Priest
Leviticus 21
Leviticus 21:1-6, 10-12
1. And the LORD said unto Moses, Speak unto the priests the sons of Aaron, and say unto them, There shall none be defiled for the dead among his people:
1. Et dixit Jehova ad Mosen, Alloquere sacerdotes filios Aharon, et dicito eis, Super animam non contaminabit se quisquam vestrum it, populis suis:
2. But for his kin that is near unto him, that is, for his mother, and for his father, and for his son, and for his daughter, and for his brother,
2. Sed super propinquo suo, propinquo sibi, nempe super matre sua, et super patre suo, et super filio suo, et super filia sua, et superfratre suo.,
3. And for his sister a virgin, that is nigh unto him, which hath had no husband; for her may he be defiled.
3. Et super sorore sua virgine propinqua sibi, quae non fuerit viro: super ea contaminabit se.
4. But he shall not defile himself, being a chief man among his people, to profane himself.
4. Non contaminabit se in principe in populis suis, ut polluat sese.
5. They shall not make baldness upon their head, neither shall they shave off the corner of their beard, nor make any cuttings in their flesh.
5. Non decalvabunt calvitium in capitc suo, et extremitatem barbae suse non radent, et in carne sua non incident ullam incisuram.
6. They shall be holy unto their God, and not profane the name of their God: for the offerings of the LORD made by fire, and the bread of their God, they do offer: therefore they shall be holy.
6. Sancti erunt Dco suo, neque polluent nomen Dei sui: quia oblationes ignitas Jehovoe, et panem Dei tui offerunt, proinde erunt sancti.
10. And he that is the high priest among his brethren, upon whose head the anointing oil was poured, and that is consecrated to put on the garments, shall not uncover his head, nor rend his clothes;
10. Sacerdos autem praecipuus inter fratres suos super cujus caput fusum fuerit oleum unctionis, et consecraverit manum suam ut induat vestes, caput suum non discooperiet, et vestes suas non scindet.
11. Neither shall he go in to any dead body, nor defile himself for his father, or for his mother;
11. Et ad omnes animas mortui non ingredietur, ne super patre quidem suo, ant matre sua, contaminabit se.
12. Neither shall he go out of the sanctuary, nor profane the sanctuary of his God; for the crown of the anointing oil of his God is upon him: I am the LORD.
12. Et de sanctuario non ingredietur, neque polluet sanctuarium Dei sui: quia corona olei unctionis Dei sui est super eum. Ego Jehova.
entries.4702db07e54b575d2b55ea64ecc7e35c2fea0f63: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.10.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.10.12" sID="gen18397" type="section"/> <div sID="gen18398" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12. </hi><hi type="italic">And Moses spake unto Aaron, and unto Eleazar</hi> Lest hereafter the priests should transgress through ignorance, Moses admonishes them of their duty; and perhaps he was moved by some immediate reason to give these particular injunctions rather than any others. As yet they were but little practiced in the observance of the rites; and what had happened to their brethren must have rendered them anxious. Now, this consternation at the death of their brethren might have so confounded their senses, that they could not apply themselves with so much composure as they ought to the service of God; and thus the offering would have been improperly made. Lest, therefore, their grief should so disturb them as to prevent the due performance of their office, he commands them to eat what remained of the meat-offering with the burnt-sacrifices. Whence we gather that he endeavored to prevent them from transgressing on that day in consequence of their minds being occupied by their recent grief. And in order to induce them to obedience, he sets before them the authority of God, to which it was fitting that the priesthood should be subject, as being founded upon it.<div eID="gen18398" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.10.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen18397" osisID="Lev.10.12" type="section"/>
entries.d7721eb719c6bd458641163b7ad5377036208539: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.10.16" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.10.16" sID="gen18399" type="section"/> <div sID="gen18400" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16. </hi><hi type="italic">And Moses diligently sought the goat of the sin-offering</hi> Moses had not omitted to tell them what was to be done with the goat; and the sacrifice which he had himself performed, was a visible instruction to them. He had set before them what they should imitate, and this would have been enough even for children. But, as I have said, in such serious matters Moses had not spared labor and care, whereas the sons of Aaron, as if they had neither heard nor seen anything of the sort, pervert the whole order of them, although they had been just before reminded that they had been appointed to keep the charge of God. Perhaps they were impelled to this error by the trouble arising from their grief; but we gather from hence that however exquisite may be the ability of masters and teachers, it may be often fruitless unless they have obedient scholars with retentive memories. And hence also we learn that when God often inculcates the same thing, His labor is not superfluous, because we do not understand what we seem to understand; or what has been clearly shewn to us soon afterwards escapes.<div eID="gen18400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18401" type="x-p"/>Further from the anger of Moses, which is mentioned in his praise, we may infer that the transgression was no light one, although it was not so severely punished as the presumption of Nadab and Abihu. The excuse which some make for them, or allege in extenuation of their crime, that they thought they were deprived of the right before accorded to them, and therefore abstained through modesty, is refuted by the answer of Aaron himself. It was, therefore, grief alone which impelled them to this error. But the reason why God was more merciful to them than to their brethren, is only known to Himself. Conjectures may, indeed, be advanced; but at last we must come to this, that because God’s judgments are hidden, they are not therefore unjust; but that we must humbly adore their depth into which the minds of men cannot penetrate.<div eID="gen18401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18402" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19. </hi><hi type="italic">And Aaron said unto Moses, Behold, this day</hi> Aaron replies that it arose from pious fear that they had not feasted before God, because they would in a manner have defiled the sanctuary by their tears and melancholy, as if he had said, Part indeed of the sin-offering was reserved for our food, but we could not properly partake of it except in cheerfulness and with thanksgiving. The grief arising from his sudden bereavement did not allow of this; but it was not a just defense; for he ought rather to have striven against the feelings of the flesh, so that his domestic calamity should not withhold him from the service of God. But, inasmuch as in his perplexity his fear was deserving of pity, Moses forgives him; and it is said that he was appeased, because he finds less of evil than he supposed.<div eID="gen18402"                   <ns0:head>CHAP. X.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 AND <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Numb. 3. 4. and 26. 61. 1 Chron. 24. 2.</ns0:note> Nadab and Abihu the sons of Aa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ron, took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, and offered strange fire <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">So called, as not appointed for, nor belonging to, the pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent work, fire not taken from the Altar as it ought, but from some common fire.</ns0:note> before the LORD <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Upon the Altar of incense.</ns0:note>, which he commanded them not <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">For see<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> himself neither did nor might do any thing in Gods worship without Gods command, which is oft noted of him, for these to do it was a more unpardonable and inexcusable pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sumption. Besides, <ns0:hi>not commanding</ns0:hi> may be here put for <ns0:hi>forbid<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ding,</ns0:hi> as it is <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 32. 35. Now as this was forbidden impli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />citly, <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 6. 12. especially when God himself, made a com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment upon that text and by sending fire from heaven declar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed of what fire he there spake, so it is more than probable it was forbidden expresly, though that be not here menti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />oned, nor was it necessary it should be.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And there went out fire from the LORD <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">From heaven, or rather from the Sanctuary. See <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 9. 24.</ns0:note>, and devoured them <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Destroyed their lives: for their bodies and garments were not consumed, as it appears from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4, 5. Thus the sword is said to <ns0:hi>devour</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2. 26. Thus lightning many times kills persons, without any hurt to their bodies or gar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments.</ns0:note>, and they died before the LORD.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Then Moses said unto Aaron, This <ns0:hi>is it</ns0:hi> that the LORD spake <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Though the express words be not recorded in Scripture, where onely the heads of Sermons and Discourses are contained, yet it is probable they were uttered by <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> in Gods name. Howsoever, the sence and substance of them is in many places. See <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19. 22. and 29. 43. <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 8. 35.</ns0:note>, saying, I will be sanctified <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This may note, either 1. their duty to sanctifie God, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> to demean them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves with such care and reverence and watchfulness as be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />comes the holiness of the God whom they serve, and of the worship in which they are engaged: whence he leaves them to gather the justice of the present judgment for their gross neglect herein. Or 2. Gods purpose to sanctifie himself, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> to declare and manifest himself to be an holy and righteous God by his severe and impartial punishment of all transgres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sors how near soever they are to him.</ns0:note> in them that come nigh me <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Who draw near to me, or to the place where I dwell, and are admitted into the holy place, whence others are shut out. It is a description of the Priests. See <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19. 22. <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 21. 17. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 42. 13, 14.</ns0:note>, and before all the people I will be glorified <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">As they have sinned publickly and scandalously so I will vindicate my honour in a publick and exemplary manner, that all men may learn to give me the glory of my soveraignty and holiness by an exact conformity to my laws.</ns0:note>: and Aaron held his peace <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Partly through excessive grief, which is sometimes signified by silence, as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 47. 5. <ns0:hi>Lam.</ns0:hi> 2. 10. and principally in acknowledgment of Gods justice and submission to it. Compare <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 39. 10. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 24. 17. He murmured not, nor replied against God, nor against <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> wisely considering that their sin was directly against God, and in that which is most dear and honourable in Gods account, to wit, in his worship; and that Gods honour ought to be dearer to him than his sons; and that this be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the first violation of the law newly given, and commit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted by those who should have been the strictest observers and assertors of it, did deserve a very severe punishment.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">For <ns0:hi>Aaron</ns0:hi> and his sons had scarce finished their consecra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion-work, and were employed in their holy ministrations, from which they were not to be called for funeral solemnities. See <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi>

                        </ns0:gap>1. 1, &c.</ns0:note> the sons of Uzziel, the uncle of Aaron <ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">See <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 6. 18. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 3. 19.</ns0:note>, and said unto them, Come near, carry your brethren <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Kinsmen, as that word is oft used, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 13. 8. and 24. 27.</ns0:note> from before the Sanctuary, out of the camp <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Where the burying places of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> were, that the living might neither be annoyed by the unwholsome sent of the dead, nor defiled by the touch of their graves.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 So they went near, and carried them in their coats <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">In the holy garments wherein they ministred, which might be done either 1. as a testimony of a respect due to them not<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />withstanding their present failure, and that God in judgment remembred mercy, and when he took away their lives, spared their souls. Or 2. because being polluted both by their sin and by the touch of their dead bodies, God would not have them any more used in his service.</ns0:note> out of the camp, as Moses had said.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And Moses said unto Aaron, and unto Elea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />zar, and unto Ithamar his sons, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Num. 6. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> Uncover not your heads <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Either 1. by putting off your Miters and Bonnets, or Or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />naments, and going bare-headed, as mourners sometimes did. See <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 13. 45. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 24. 17, 23. Or 2. by shaving off the hair of your heads and beards, as mourners did. See <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 1. 20. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 7. 29. and 41. 5. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 4<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 20. <ns0:hi>Mich.</ns0:hi> 1. 16. This latter may seem to be principally intended, 1. because this ce<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />remony of <ns0:hi>uncovering the head</ns0:hi> being used by the people as well as by the Priests in case of mourning, as the places now al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledged shew, and the other ceremony here joyned with it of <ns0:hi>rending the clothes,</ns0:hi> being also common to the people, seems to imply that he speaks not of that uncovering the head which was peculiar to the Priests, but to that which was common both to Priests and people, especially seeing that which is here forbidden to these Priests is in the following words allowed to the people, to <ns0:hi>bewail</ns0:hi> their death, which as at other times it was, so now probably might be performed by these same cere<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monies. 2. because the High-priest is forbidden to <ns0:hi>uncover his head</ns0:hi> in way of mourning for the dead<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> not onely at that time when he was in actual ministration, but at all times, even when he had neither his miter nor any of the holy garments upon him, <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 21. 10.</ns0:note>, neither rend your clothes <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Give no signification of your sorrow, mourn not for them, partly lest you should seem to justifie and approve of your brethren and tacitly reflect upon God as too se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vere in his proceedings with them; and partly least thereby you should be diverted from or disturbed in your present ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vice, which God expects should be done chearfully.</ns0:note>, lest you die, and lest wrath come upon all the peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple: but let your brethren, the whole house of Israel bewail the burning which the LORD hath kindled <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Not so much in compassion to them against whom I have shewed such great and just indignation, as in sorrow for the tokens of Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine displeasure.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And ye shall not go out from the door of the tabernacle of the congregation <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Where at this time they were, either because this happened within the 7 days of their consecration: See <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 8. 35. or because they were longer detained there about some other holy mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />strations. Though the former may seem more probable, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause the <ns0:hi>meat-offering</ns0:hi> here mentioned, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 12. and the <ns0:hi>sin-of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fering, ver.</ns0:hi> 16. were part of the consecration-offerings.</ns0:note>, lest you die: for the anointing oil of the LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> upon you <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">You are persons consecrated peculiarly to Gods service, which there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore it is just and reasonable you should prefer before all fune<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral solemnities.</ns0:note>: and they did according to the word of Moses.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And the LORD spake unto Aaron, say<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ezek. 44. 21. 1 Tim. 3. 3.</ns0:note> Do not drink wine nor strong drink <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">This is here added, either because <ns0:hi>Nadab</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Abihu</ns0:hi> had been led to their errour by drinking too much, which might easily fall out when they were feasting and full of joy for their entrance into so honourable and profitable an employment; or at lest because others might thereby be drawn to commit the same miscarriages, which they might now commit from other causes. Drunkenness is so odious a sin in it self, especially in a Minister, and most of all in the time of his administration of sacred things, that God saw fit to prevent all occasions of it. And hence the Devil, who is Gods ape in his prescriptions for his worship, required this abstinence from his Priests in their Idolatrous services.</ns0:note>; thou, nor thy sons with thee, when ye go into the tabernacle of the congregation, lest ye die: <ns0:hi>It shall be</ns0:hi> a statute for ever throughout your ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nerations:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And that ye may <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 15. 19. Ezek. 22. 26. and 44. 23.</ns0:note> put difference between holy and unholy <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Persons and things, which <ns0:hi>Nadab</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Abihu</ns0:hi> did not, mista<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />king unholy or common fire for that which was sacred and ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pointed by God for their use.</ns0:note>, and between unclean and clean.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And that ye may teach <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Be apt to teach aright<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> which dr<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>nken persons are very unfit to do.</ns0:note> the children of Israel all the statutes which the LORD hath spo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken unto them by the hand of Moses.<ns0:gap reason="missing" extent="2+ pages">

                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:93" />25 And whosoever beareth <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>taketh away,</ns0:hi> out of the place where haply it may ly, by which others may be either offended, or polluted.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>ought</ns0:hi> of the car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cass of them, shall wash his clothes, and be unclean until the even.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 <ns0:hi>The carcasses</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Which word is easily to be understood out of <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 24. and 25. where it is expressed.</ns0:note> of every beast which divid<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth the hoof, and <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> not cloven footed, nor chew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth the cud, <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> unclean unto you: every one that toucheth them, shall be unclean.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And whatsoever goeth upon his paws <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>upon his hands; i. e.</ns0:hi> which hath feet divided into se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veral parts like fingers, as dogs, cats, apes, bears, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mong all manner of beasts, that go on <ns0:hi>all</ns0:hi> four, those <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> unclean unto you: whoso toucheth their carcass, shall be unclean until the even.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 And he that beareth the carcass of them, shall wash his clothes, and be unclean until the even: they <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> unclean unto you.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 These also <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> unclean unto you, among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the Weasel, and the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 66. 17.</ns0:note> Mouse, and the Tortois after his kind,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 And the Ferret, and the Camelion, and the Lyzard, and the Snail, and the Mole.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 These <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> unclean to you among all that creep: whosoever doth touch them when they be dead, shall be unclean until the even.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 And upon whatsoever <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> of them, when they are dead, doth fall, it shall be unclean, whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther <ns0:hi>it be</ns0:hi> any vessel of wood, or rayment, or skin, or sack, whatsoever vessel <ns0:hi>it be,</ns0:hi> wherein <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> work is done, it must be put into water, and it shall be unclean until the even: so it shall be cleansed.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 And every earthen vessel, whereinto <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> of them falleth, whatsoever <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in it shall be unclean, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 6. 28.</ns0:note> ye shall break it.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="34">34 Of all meat which may be eaten, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> on which <ns0:hi>such</ns0:hi> water cometh <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The meaning is, that flesh or herbs or other food which is dressed in water, to wit, in a vessel so polluted, shall be unclean, not so, if it be food which is eaten dry, as bread, fruits, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> the reason of which difference seems to be this, that the water did sooner receive the pollution in it self, and convey it to the food so dressed.</ns0:note>, shall be unclean: And all drink that may be drunk in every <ns0:hi>such</ns0:hi> vessel, shall be unclean.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="35">35 And every <ns0:hi>thing</ns0:hi> whereupon <ns0:hi>any part</ns0:hi> of their carcass falleth, shall be unclean, <ns0:hi>whether it be</ns0:hi> oven, or ranges for pots, they shall be broken down: <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> they <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> unclean, and shall be unclean unto you.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="37">37 And if <ns0:hi>any part</ns0:hi> of their carcass fall upon any sowing seed which is to be sown <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Partly because this was necessary provision for man; and partly because such seed would not be used for mans food till it had received many alterations in the earth, whereby such pol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lution was taken away.                   <ns0:p n="38">38 But if <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> water be put upon the seed <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The reason of the difference is, partly because wet seed doth sooner receive and longer retain any pollution; and partly because such seed was not fit to be sown presently, and therefore that necessity which justified the use of the dry seed which was speedily to be sown could not be pretended in this case.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:hi>any part</ns0:hi> of their carcass fall thereof, it <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> unclean unto you.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="39">39 And if any beast of which ye may eat, die <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either of it self, or being killed by some wild beast, in which cases the blood was not poured forth, as it was when they were killed by men either for food or sacrifice.</ns0:note>, he that toucheth the carcass thereof, shall be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clean until the even.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="44">44 For <ns0:hi>I am</ns0:hi> the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctifie your selves, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 19. 2. and 20. 7. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
